title: Compass Bearing Visualizer: See Both Bearings
description: See the initial and reverse bearing between two places drawn on the map with the Compass Bearing Visualizer, with distance in miles and km. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, Heathrow to JFK starts at approx. 287.9° — visibly northwest on the compass rose — even though New York feels like it should be 'straight across' the Atlantic.
quick_answer: The Compass Bearing Visualizer draws the direction between two places so you can see it, not only read it: the initial great-circle bearing one way, the reverse bearing for the return, and the distance, all on the map and compass rose. It is the visual companion to a bearing calculation.
steps_intro: Bearings confuse people as numbers; as a picture they explain themselves. Two steps:

body.t: Show a class the rose turning as the destination moves, and the difference between initial and reverse bearings stops being a formula and becomes something they can point at.
Before walking a bearing from the
, sight the same line here: if the drawn direction disagrees with your expectation, one of the two points is wrong — find out indoors.
A visual check that the short path to a distant station really does leave over the neighbour's roof in that direction saves a return trip up the ladder.
A drawn bearing communicates in a briefing what three spoken numbers cannot: where the journey starts out pointing, and why it is not the direction of the destination on a flat wall map.

JFK → Heathrow starts at approx. 51.4° (northeast); Heathrow → JFK starts at 287.9° (west-northwest). On the visualizer the two roses are plainly not opposites — the single clearest picture of great-circle geometry in this whole section.
Heathrow → Paris CDG starts at approx. 140.9° (southeast) and the return at 323.2° (northwest). Even at 347 km the asymmetry is visible, just smaller — the effect never fully switches off.

faq: Is this the same as the Bearing Calculator?

It computes the same spherical bearings; the difference is presentation. The calculator leads with numbers, this tool leads with the drawn line and compass rose. Many people check a number here before trusting it.
Does the rose show magnetic north?
No — bearings are true (from geographic north). A handheld compass reads magnetic north; apply your local declination before using a drawn bearing outdoors.
Why is the line between the points curved?
Because the shortest surface path is a great circle, which a flat map projection bends. The bearing shown is the direction at the start of that curved path.
Can I read the bearing at the destination instead?
The reverse bearing is exactly that perspective: the direction you would set off on from the destination to come back. Both are drawn so you can compare them.
What bearing is due west on the rose?
270°. Points run clockwise from north: 0° N, 90° E, 180° S, 270° W, with the sixteen named points spaced 22.5° apart.
Does it work for two points in the same town?
Yes. At short range the curve flattens and the bearing behaves like the flat-map direction — the visual check is still the fastest way to catch a swapped point.
Can I use coordinates instead of searching?
Yes — set either point by coordinates or by clicking the map when a named search is ambiguous.
